chapter: The 1920s road: dance style and management
title: Heel and toe, and dancing the melody
summary: He added the heel to toe-only tapping and danced songs like Old Man River so the words could almost be recognized; the sound of the taps was the point.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: How about your steps what made them different? Were you using your whole toe and your heel differently?
No, I was using both my heel and toe. Everybody else was just using their toe and I was doing the heel and toe. That's what I added to the dancing, the heel.
What about the kinds of rhythms that you added to the music? Were you doing it a different way than other people were?
What kind of rhythms that you were producing with your feet that went along with the music, the way you were approaching dancing in relationship to jazz music, was it different than other people's?
Oh, yeah, sure it was, sure it was.

In every sense, in every sense. You see, I would do more or less a song when dancing, the melody. I could do "Ole Man River" dancing and you could almost tell the words, the way I danced it. I'd do "Sweet Sue," any song you take I would do it in dancing
so you could almost tell that's it. You understand what I'm saying?
So it was really the sound that you were making.
Your dancing was not only visual but you were doing something different with sounds.
That's right, that's exactly it. So why I'm trying to explain that song that I was telling to go places, see faces --

See the smile on my face
From the sound of the beat
From the taps on my feet

That's what is in that song --'From the sound and the beat and the taps on my feet, that's it, taps of my feet.' That's why I wanted to do that song, to express that exactly and the smile would come from the people hearing what I'm doing to make them smile. See, that's why I wanted to do that for, that song. But I didn't get around to it. I guess some day. I
